title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 11
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Lab Fee Charged Twice
listeningScripts.text: Student: Hi, I'm calling about my tuition account. I think I've been charged the lab fee twice for the same course. Clerk: I can look into that. Can I have your student number? Student: It's four-oh-two-nine-one-seven. Clerk: Thank you. And which course? Student: Biology two-ten. The lab fee is one hundred and forty dollars, and it shows up on my statement for both September and October. Clerk: I see two entries, yes. Sometimes the second one is a deposit rather than a duplicate, but in this case both are coded as lab fees. When did you notice? Student: Yesterday, when I was applying for my student loan. The loan office said my balance looked too high. Clerk: That would do it. I can submit a correction request today. It takes about ten business days to clear off your account, though the money moves back to your card sooner than that. Four days, usually. Student: Will I still be able to register for the winter term while it's pending? The registration deadline is the twenty-second. Clerk: You will, as long as your balance is under five hundred dollars. Right now it shows six hundred and twenty. Once the correction goes through it drops to four hundred and eighty. Student: So I have to wait for it to clear before I can register. Clerk: Not necessarily. I can put a note on your file so registration isn't blocked, and that takes effect this afternoon rather than in ten days. But you'd need to email the registrar's office from your student address to confirm you're asking for it. Student: I'll do that as soon as we hang up. Do I need to attach anything? Clerk: Just your student number and the course code. No screenshots — we can see the statement from our side.

listeningScripts.title: Planning a Winter Camping Trip
listeningScripts.text: A: So are we actually doing this? Camping. In February. B: I've already booked it. Two nights, the weekend of the fourteenth. A: The fourteenth. You've booked us a romantic weekend in a snowbank. B: It was the only weekend the yurts were free. And they're heated — there's a wood stove in each one. A: A yurt is not camping. B: It's camping if you have to carry your own water in, which we do. The tap at the site is shut off until April. A: How far is it from the parking lot? B: Four hundred metres or so. But the trail isn't ploughed, so we'll want the sled for the jugs and the food. A: Fine. What am I responsible for? B: Food for four meals, and your own sleeping bag. The yurt has bunks but no bedding. I'll bring the stove fuel and the water. A: What about the dog? B: Dogs are allowed on the site but not inside the yurts. So, no dog. A: No dog. B: My sister said she'd take him. She owes us for August. A: Then I'm in. What's the cancellation policy, just in case one of us breaks a leg? B: Full refund up to seven days before. After that we lose the whole thing.

listeningScripts.title: Community Garden Plot Orientation
listeningScripts.text: Welcome, everyone, and congratulations on getting a plot. We had two hundred and forty applications this year for eighty-six plots, so the wait list is not a formality. A few things before you start digging. Your plot number is on the stake at the corner. Plots run for one season, April to October, and if you want the same plot next year you do have to reapply — but returning gardeners get priority, as long as the plot passed inspection. There are two inspections: early July and mid-September. We are looking for two things only. Is the plot planted, and are the paths around it clear? A plot that is still bare at the July inspection goes back to the wait list. Water. The taps at either end of the site are turned on from the first of May. Hoses are shared, and they go back on the rack coiled — every year we lose two or three to being left out in the sun. Watering is by hand or watering can only. No sprinklers, because the pressure drops for everyone else on the site. Tools live in the green shed. The code is on the card in your welcome envelope. It is not on the noticeboard, and please do not write it on the noticeboard. Compost goes in the bays at the north end. The two bays on the left take green waste; the one on the right is finished compost, and you are welcome to take what you need from it. Diseased tomato plants do not go in any of the bays — those go in the city bin by the gate, or the disease comes back next season. Last thing. The harvest table by the shed is for surplus. Anything still on it on a Sunday evening goes to the food bank on Monday morning.

listeningScripts.title: Newfoundland Ferry Service Adds Winter Sailings
listeningScripts.text: The provincial ferry service will run winter crossings to the south coast communities for the first time in eleven years, under a decision announced this morning. Two sailings a week will operate from the first of December to the end of March. They replace the present arrangement, in which residents depend on a chartered flight whenever the weather allows it. Transport officials say those flights were cancelled on roughly one day in three last winter. The vessel assigned to the route, the Marine Voyager, has been refitted at a cost of eleven million dollars, most of it spent on strengthening the hull against ice. It carries a hundred and forty passengers and twelve vehicles. Not everyone is satisfied. The mayor of one of the communities told reporters that two sailings a week is half what her council asked for, and that the published schedule leaves a five-day gap over the Christmas period. The department says the timetable will be reviewed in February, once it has a full season of demand figures. Bookings open on the fifteenth of November.

listeningScripts.title: Sunday Parking Charges Downtown
listeningScripts.text: Reyes: The proposal is straightforward. Metered parking downtown is free on Sundays. We would charge two dollars an hour, the same as Saturday, and the revenue — about four hundred thousand a year — goes to the sidewalk repair fund. Whitfield: And my Sunday trade goes with it. I run a bakery on Ninth. Sunday is my second-busiest day, and most of my customers drive in from the east side, because there is no bus that gets them here before eleven. Okonjo: That is the actual problem, though, isn't it. Sunday bus service is the thinnest of the week. If we spent that four hundred thousand on Sunday frequency instead of sidewalks, Dana's customers would have a way in that doesn't need a parking space at all. Whitfield: In three years, maybe. My lease is up in eighteen months. Reyes: I would note the charge only applies between ten and four. Early morning and evening stay free. Whitfield: My rush is eleven to two. That is exactly the window. Okonjo: Which is also when the spaces are fullest and people circle the block looking for one. Pricing them is how you get turnover. At the moment somebody parks at nine-thirty and leaves at three. Whitfield: Then cap the stay instead of charging for it. A two-hour limit does the same thing without taking money out of my customers' pockets. Reyes: A time limit needs enforcement officers working Sundays, and that costs more than it brings in. We modelled it — about sixty thousand a year net loss. Okonjo: I could live with the charge if the revenue were split. Half to sidewalks, half to Sunday buses. Reyes: That I can take to council. Whitfield: And I would want the free period widened to eleven before I supported any of it.

listeningScripts.title: The Four-Day School Week
listeningScripts.text: Districts across North America have been shortening the school week, usually to four longer days with either Friday or Monday off. The number doing it has roughly quadrupled since twenty-ten, and almost all of them are rural. I want to look at why they do it, and whether the reasons hold up. The stated reason is nearly always money. Closing the buildings one day a week saves on heating, on bus fuel, and on the hourly staff who are not needed when the students are not there. Those savings are real, but they are small. The studies I trust put them between half a per cent and two and a half per cent of a district's budget. That is not nothing. It is also not the rescue it is sometimes described as. The stronger argument is one districts talk about less: hiring. In a town competing with a city an hour away for the same teachers, a four-day week is a benefit that costs nothing on paper. Several superintendents have told researchers they received applications they would not otherwise have seen. If you cannot put a teacher in the classroom at all, the quality of the timetable inside it is beside the point. Now the cost. Results on achievement are mixed, and mixed is worse than it sounds, because the effects are not spread evenly. Older students appear to be roughly unaffected. Younger ones lose ground, and so do students whose families cannot arrange care on the fifth day — and those two groups overlap heavily. A four-day week moves a day of supervision from the school to the household, and households differ enormously in what they can absorb. So my position is this. Do it for hiring, if you do it at all, and say plainly that is the reason. Do not do it for the budget, because the savings are too small to justify how the costs land. And if you do it, fund the fifth day for the families who need it. Otherwise you have not saved money. You have moved the bill to the households least able to pay it.

questions.prompt: Why is the student calling?
options: A lab fee was charged for a course the student dropped
The student's loan application was refused
The same lab fee has been charged twice
The registration deadline has already passed
questions.correctAnswer: The same lab fee has been charged twice
questions.explanation: The student opens by saying the lab fee appears for the same course twice, and the clerk confirms both entries are coded as lab fees.

questions.prompt: How much is the lab fee?
questions.explanation: The student gives the fee as one hundred and forty dollars. The other figures are the corrected balance, the registration threshold and the current balance.

questions.prompt: How did the student find out about the problem?
options: The registrar's office telephoned
While applying for a student loan
A lecturer mentioned it in class
An email arrived from the billing department
questions.correctAnswer: While applying for a student loan
questions.explanation: The student noticed it the day before while applying for a loan, after the loan office said the balance looked too high.

questions.prompt: How soon does the clerk say the money will be back on the card?
options: The same afternoon
In ten business days
On the twenty-second
In about four days
questions.correctAnswer: In about four days
questions.explanation: The clerk separates the two timings: about ten business days to clear the account, but roughly four for the money to reach the card.

questions.prompt: What must the balance be below for the student to register?
questions.explanation: The clerk gives five hundred dollars as the registration threshold. Four hundred and eighty is what the balance becomes once corrected, which is why it clears the threshold.

questions.prompt: What does the clerk suggest as the faster way to protect the student's registration?
options: Paying the disputed amount and claiming it back later
Registering before the correction is submitted
Asking the loan office to contact the registrar
Adding a note to the file, which takes effect the same afternoon
questions.correctAnswer: Adding a note to the file, which takes effect the same afternoon
questions.explanation: The clerk offers the note as an alternative to waiting the ten days, and says it takes effect that afternoon.

questions.prompt: What must the student's email contain?
options: A copy of the statement
The loan office's reference number
The student number and the course code
The date of the original payment
questions.correctAnswer: The student number and the course code
questions.explanation: The clerk asks only for the student number and the course code.

questions.prompt: What does the clerk say is not needed?
options: Screenshots of the account
A phone call to confirm the email
The student's home address
A signature on a printed form
questions.correctAnswer: Screenshots of the account
questions.explanation: The clerk says no screenshots, because the billing office can see the statement itself.

questions.prompt: Which weekend has been booked?
options: The first weekend of April
The weekend of the fourteenth
The weekend after the fourteenth
The last weekend of February
questions.correctAnswer: The weekend of the fourteenth
questions.explanation: B says the booking is for two nights on the weekend of the fourteenth.

questions.prompt: Why did B choose that weekend?
options: It was the cheapest weekend of the month
It was the only weekend both were free
The trail is ploughed at that time of year
It was the only one with a yurt available
questions.correctAnswer: It was the only one with a yurt available
questions.explanation: B says plainly that it was the only weekend the yurts were free, and the romantic date is a coincidence A teases about.

questions.prompt: Why will they need the sled?
options: The trail from the parking lot is not cleared of snow
The yurt is more than a kilometre from the road
The dog cannot walk that far in the cold
The water jugs are too heavy for one person
questions.correctAnswer: The trail from the parking lot is not cleared of snow
questions.explanation: B says the trail isn't ploughed, which is why the sled is needed for the jugs and food across the four hundred metres.

questions.prompt: What is A being asked to bring?
options: Stove fuel and the water jugs
Bedding for the bunks and a sled
Food for four meals and a sleeping bag
Food for two days and a wood stove
questions.correctAnswer: Food for four meals and a sleeping bag
questions.explanation: A brings food and a sleeping bag; B brings the stove fuel and the water. The yurt has bunks but no bedding.

questions.prompt: What is the cancellation policy?
options: A refund is given only for medical reasons
A full refund is given up to seven days beforehand
Half the cost is refunded at any point
There is no refund once the booking is made
questions.correctAnswer: A full refund is given up to seven days beforehand
questions.explanation: B says full refund up to seven days before, and nothing afterwards.

questions.prompt: How many plots were available this year?
options: Two hundred and forty
Two or three
One hundred and fifty-four
Eighty-six
questions.correctAnswer: Eighty-six
questions.explanation: There were two hundred and forty applications for eighty-six plots.

questions.prompt: What gives a returning gardener priority for the same plot?
options: Having held the plot for more than one season
Their plot passed inspection
Applying before the first of May
Volunteering at the harvest table
questions.correctAnswer: Their plot passed inspection
questions.explanation: Returning gardeners get priority provided the plot passed inspection, and they still have to reapply.

questions.prompt: What happens to a plot that is still bare in July?
options: It is returned to the wait list
The gardener is given until September to plant it
A fee is charged for the following season
The paths around it are cleared by staff
questions.correctAnswer: It is returned to the wait list
questions.explanation: A plot still bare at the July inspection goes back to the wait list.

questions.prompt: What is the rule about watering?
options: Only before the first of May
Only from the taps at the north end
Only by hand or watering can
Sprinklers are allowed outside peak hours
questions.correctAnswer: Only by hand or watering can
questions.explanation: Watering is by hand or watering can only. Sprinklers are ruled out because they drop the pressure for everyone else.

questions.prompt: Where can gardeners find the code for the shed?
options: On the noticeboard by the gate
On the stake at the corner of the plot
From any returning gardener
On a card in the welcome envelope
questions.correctAnswer: On a card in the welcome envelope
questions.explanation: The code is on the card in the welcome envelope, and the speaker asks twice that it not be written on the noticeboard.

questions.prompt: Where should diseased tomato plants be put?
options: In the two bays on the left
In the city bin by the gate
In the bay on the right
On the harvest table
questions.correctAnswer: In the city bin by the gate
questions.explanation: Diseased tomato plants go in the city bin by the gate rather than in any compost bay, or the disease returns the following season.

questions.prompt: What is being announced?
options: A new ferry vessel built for the south coast
The end of chartered flights to the region
Winter ferry crossings for the first time in eleven years
A year-round ferry service to the south coast
questions.correctAnswer: Winter ferry crossings for the first time in eleven years
questions.explanation: The service will run winter crossings for the first time in eleven years; the vessel is refitted rather than new, and the sailings run December to March rather than all year.

questions.prompt: How have residents travelled in winter until now?
options: By chartered flight when the weather allowed
By a reduced ferry timetable
By road around the coast
They have not travelled in winter
questions.correctAnswer: By chartered flight when the weather allowed
questions.explanation: Residents depended on a chartered flight whenever the weather allowed, and those flights were cancelled about one day in three last winter.

questions.prompt: What was most of the eleven million dollars spent on?
options: Building a new terminal
Increasing the vehicle capacity
Training additional crew
Strengthening the hull against ice
questions.correctAnswer: Strengthening the hull against ice
questions.explanation: Most of the refit cost went on strengthening the hull against ice.

questions.prompt: What is the mayor's objection?
options: The vessel is too small for the number of vehicles
The number of sailings is half what her council requested
Bookings open too late in the year
The refit cost too much public money
questions.correctAnswer: The number of sailings is half what her council requested
questions.explanation: The mayor says two sailings a week is half what the council asked for, and separately points to the five-day gap at Christmas.

questions.prompt: When will the timetable be looked at again?
options: On the fifteenth of November
At the end of March
In February
Once the vessel is refitted
questions.correctAnswer: In February
questions.explanation: The department says the timetable will be reviewed in February, once a full season of demand figures exists.

questions.prompt: What is being proposed?
options: Raising the Saturday parking charge to match Sunday
Charging two dollars an hour for Sunday parking downtown
Removing the meters from downtown streets
Closing Ninth Street to traffic on Sundays
questions.correctAnswer: Charging two dollars an hour for Sunday parking downtown
questions.explanation: Reyes opens with the proposal: Sunday metered parking, charged at the Saturday rate of two dollars an hour.

questions.prompt: Why does Whitfield object to the charge?
options: Her customers have no way of paying at a meter
The bakery has no parking of its own
Sunday is the only day she opens
The charging hours cover her busiest period
questions.correctAnswer: The charging hours cover her busiest period
questions.explanation: Reyes says the charge applies from ten to four; Whitfield answers that her rush is eleven to two, which sits inside that window. Sunday is her second-busiest day, not her only one.

questions.prompt: What does Okonjo say the real problem is?
options: The sidewalk repair fund is too small
Too many people drive in from the east side
Sunday bus service is too infrequent
Parking is priced too low on Saturdays
questions.correctAnswer: Sunday bus service is too infrequent
questions.explanation: Okonjo calls the thin Sunday bus service the actual problem, and would spend the revenue on frequency rather than sidewalks.

questions.prompt: Why does Whitfield reject the transit argument?
options: Better service would arrive too late for her lease
Her customers would not use buses in any case
She would rather the money went to sidewalk repairs
The money would come out of her taxes
questions.correctAnswer: Better service would arrive too late for her lease
questions.explanation: Whitfield answers that better service might come in three years, while her lease has eighteen months to run.

questions.prompt: What does Whitfield suggest instead of a charge?
options: Free parking for customers of local shops
A two-hour limit on how long a car may stay
Moving the charging window to the afternoon
A charge that applies only to non-residents
questions.correctAnswer: A two-hour limit on how long a car may stay
questions.explanation: Whitfield proposes capping the stay at two hours, which she argues produces turnover without costing her customers money.

questions.prompt: Why does Reyes reject that suggestion?
options: Two hours is too short for most visitors
The city cannot legally set time limits
It would not create enough turnover
Enforcing it on Sundays would cost more than it raised
questions.correctAnswer: Enforcing it on Sundays would cost more than it raised
questions.explanation: Reyes says a time limit needs Sunday enforcement officers, modelled at about sixty thousand a year net loss.

questions.prompt: What compromise does Okonjo offer?
options: Splitting the revenue between sidewalks and Sunday buses
Delaying the charge until bus frequency improves
Charging one dollar an hour rather than two
Exempting the east side from the charge
questions.correctAnswer: Splitting the revenue between sidewalks and Sunday buses
questions.explanation: Okonjo says he could accept the charge if the revenue were split half to sidewalks and half to Sunday buses, and Reyes agrees to take that to council.

questions.prompt: What does Whitfield say she would need before supporting the plan?
options: A share of the revenue for Ninth Street businesses
A guarantee that the rate will not rise
The free period extended to eleven o'clock
The charge limited to the summer months
questions.correctAnswer: The free period extended to eleven o'clock
questions.explanation: Whitfield's closing condition is that the free period be widened to eleven, which would move the charge off the start of her rush.

questions.prompt: What reason do districts usually give for the change?
options: It improves results for younger students
Families have asked for a longer weekend
It shortens the bus routes
It saves money
questions.correctAnswer: It saves money
questions.explanation: The speaker says the stated reason is nearly always money — heating, bus fuel and hourly staff.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker think of those savings?
options: They are usually exaggerated to the point of being invented
They are genuine but smaller than commonly claimed
They are larger in rural districts than urban ones
They are much the same in every district that has tried it
questions.correctAnswer: They are genuine but smaller than commonly claimed
questions.explanation: The speaker puts the savings at between half a per cent and two and a half per cent of a budget: real, but not the rescue it is sometimes described as.

questions.prompt: Which argument does the speaker find stronger?
options: That it helps districts recruit teachers
That it gives students more time to study
That it reduces the cost of school transport
That rural districts have no alternative
questions.correctAnswer: That it helps districts recruit teachers
questions.explanation: The speaker calls hiring the stronger argument, and one districts talk about less: a four-day week is a benefit that costs nothing on paper.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say that mixed results are worse than they sound?
options: The studies contradict one another entirely
Districts stop measuring after the first year
The effects fall unevenly on particular groups of students
The results improve only in the longer term
questions.correctAnswer: The effects fall unevenly on particular groups of students
questions.explanation: Mixed is worse than it sounds because the effects are not spread evenly — younger students and those without care on the fifth day lose ground, and the two groups overlap.

questions.prompt: Which students appear to be largely unaffected?
options: Students in urban districts
Students whose families can pay for care
Students who were already behind
Older students
questions.correctAnswer: Older students
questions.explanation: The speaker says older students appear to be roughly unaffected, and identifies younger students as the ones who lose ground.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's overall position?
options: Adopt it wherever a district's budget is under strain
Adopt it for hiring, and pay for care on the fifth day
Avoid it in rural districts and allow it elsewhere
Delay it until the achievement evidence is settled
questions.correctAnswer: Adopt it for hiring, and pay for care on the fifth day
questions.explanation: The speaker's closing position is to do it for hiring rather than for the budget, and to fund the fifth day for families who need it — otherwise the bill has simply moved to the households least able to pay.
